intro: A child in Kenya sleeps under a treated net. A grandmother in Okinawa tends her garden at ninety-five. A teenager in Chicago walks past three fast-food places on the way home. Each scene is part of global health: the study of what makes people sick or well across the whole world, and what can be done about it.

In this unit you will look at two big kinds of disease. Infectious diseases, such as malaria, TB, HIV, cholera, measles and polio, are caused by germs and spread between people. Chronic diseases, such as heart disease, stroke, cancer and diabetes, grow slowly and are shaped by daily habits and surroundings. For both, you will see that money, geography and culture matter as much as medicine.

By the end, you will be able to explain how several major diseases spread and how they are prevented or treated. You will compare the roles of global health groups, read health data, and weigh evidence about diet and lifestyle. You will also be able to argue, with facts, about what does the most good for the most people.
bigQuestion: What does it take to help people everywhere live longer, healthier lives?

title: Global Health

chapters.title: Diseases That Shape the World
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do some infections still take millions of lives when we already know how to prevent or treat them?

story.title: A Net Over the Crib
story.kicker: In western Kenya, a health worker shows a young mother how a simple net can guard her baby through the night.
paragraphs: The sun is going down over a village near Lake Victoria in western Kenya. Grace, a community health worker, walks down a dirt path with a canvas bag on her shoulder. Inside are folded blue nets. She knocks on the door of a small house where a mother is rocking her six-month-old son.

Grace unfolds a net and ties its corners to the rafters above the crib. She tucks the edges under the thin mattress so there are no gaps. The net is treated with an insecticide, she explains. A mosquito that lands on it will not live long enough to bite anyone else.

The mother asks why the net matters so much. Grace tells her that malaria is carried by mosquitoes that bite mostly at night. Babies and young children are the most likely to become very sick from it. A net over the bed every night, she says, is one of the cheapest and best protections there is.

Before she leaves, Grace writes the family's name in her notebook. She will come back next month to check the net for holes and to see how the baby is growing. Across Africa, well over a billion nets like this one have been handed out since the early 2000s. Doctors, scientists, donors and workers like Grace are all part of the same effort.
story.think: Grace's tool is a net, not a medicine. Why might a simple, cheap tool matter as much as a new drug in fighting a disease?

lessons.title: A Parasite Carried by Mosquitoes
lessons.mainIdea: Malaria is caused by a tiny parasite that female Anopheles mosquitoes pass from person to person.
reading: When a mosquito bites a person who has malaria, it sucks up blood that holds a tiny living thing called *Plasmodium*. This one-celled *parasite* grows inside the mosquito for about one to two weeks. When that mosquito bites someone else, it injects the parasite along with its saliva. Only female mosquitoes of the Anopheles group spread malaria, because only females drink blood.

Inside the new person, the parasite travels first to the liver, where it multiplies. Then it bursts into the blood and invades red blood cells. The cells break open in waves, which causes the fever, chills and sweating that malaria is known for. Severe malaria can damage the brain and other organs, and young children are most at risk.

For a long time people blamed bad air for the disease. The name malaria comes from Italian words meaning bad air. In 1880 the French army doctor Alphonse Laveran saw the parasite in a patient's blood. In 1897 the British doctor Ronald Ross showed that mosquitoes carry it. Both men later won Nobel Prizes for this work.

words.d: the group of one-celled parasites that cause malaria
a living thing that lives in or on another living thing and takes food from it
a living thing, such as a mosquito, that carries a disease from one host to another

look.title: Following the Parasite
look.text: Picture three stops on a journey. Stop one: a mosquito drinks blood from a sick person. Stop two: the parasite grows inside the mosquito for about ten days. Stop three: the mosquito bites a healthy child while she sleeps, and the parasite heads for her liver.
look.prompt: At which stop could a bed net break the chain? At which stop could a drug that kills parasites in the blood help?

check.q: What causes malaria?
choices: A virus in the air near swamps
A lack of vitamins in the diet
check.why: The reading explains that malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a one-celled parasite.

check.q: Why do only female Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria?
choices: Only females can fly at night
check.why: Only female mosquitoes drink blood, so only they can pick up and pass on the parasite.

check.q: What did Ronald Ross show in 1897?
choices: That mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite
That malaria comes from bad air
That malaria is caused by a virus
check.why: Ross showed that mosquitoes carry the parasite, replacing the old bad-air idea.

lessons.title: Nets and Sprays
lessons.mainIdea: Insecticide-treated bed nets and indoor spraying stop mosquitoes from biting, which prevents many malaria cases.
reading: Anopheles mosquitoes bite mostly between dusk and dawn, when people are asleep. That fact gives health workers a clear target. An *insecticide-treated net* hangs over a bed like a small tent. It blocks bites, and the chemical on it kills or weakens mosquitoes that land on it.

Large studies in Africa during the 1990s found that treated nets lowered child deaths in the areas that used them. Since then, well over a billion nets have been handed out, often for free. Another method is *indoor residual spraying*, where workers spray the inside walls of homes. Mosquitoes that rest on the walls after feeding are killed.

These tools face a problem. In many places mosquitoes have become resistant to common insecticides, so the chemicals work less well. Scientists answer by making nets with two different chemicals and by switching sprays. Nets also wear out and must be replaced every few years. Prevention works only if it keeps going.

words.d: a bed net coated with a chemical that kills or weakens mosquitoes
spraying insecticide on the inside walls of homes, where mosquitoes rest
when a germ or insect is no longer harmed by a chemical or drug that used to work

look.title: Two Villages
look.text: Village A received new nets five years ago, and no one has replaced them. Many have holes. Village B received nets three years ago and gets new ones every three years. A health worker checks them each month.
look.prompt: Which village would you expect to have fewer malaria cases this year? Use two facts from the reading to explain why.

check.q: Why are bed nets a good match for Anopheles mosquitoes?
choices: The mosquitoes only bite in daylight
The nets cure people who are already sick
The mosquitoes bite mostly at night while people sleep
The nets make the parasite resistant
check.why: Anopheles mosquitoes bite mostly between dusk and dawn, so a net over a sleeping person blocks them.

check.q: What is indoor residual spraying?
choices: Spraying insecticide on the walls inside homes
Spraying medicine into a patient's nose
Spraying water on crops to drown larvae
Spraying perfume to hide a person's smell
check.why: Indoor residual spraying puts insecticide on inside walls where mosquitoes rest.

check.q: What problem makes some nets and sprays work less well?
choices: Mosquitoes have become resistant to common insecticides
Nets are too expensive to make
check.why: The reading says insecticide resistance has made some chemicals less effective.

lessons.title: From an Ancient Text to a Nobel Prize
lessons.mainIdea: Artemisinin, a key malaria drug, was found by testing a plant named in an old Chinese medical text, and new vaccines now add protection.
reading: In 1969 the Chinese scientist Tu Youyou was asked to search for a new malaria drug. Older drugs such as chloroquine were failing because the parasite had become resistant. Her team read through old Chinese medical books. They tested hundreds of plant extracts. One plant, sweet wormwood, called qinghao in Chinese, looked promising.

At first the extract worked poorly. Tu noticed that a text by Ge Hong, written about 1,600 years earlier, said to soak the plant in water, with no boiling. Her team switched to a low-heat method, and the extract became powerful. They isolated the active substance, *artemisinin*, in the early 1970s. Tu Youyou shared the Nobel Prize in 2015.

Today doctors treat malaria with artemisinin-based combination therapy, which pairs artemisinin with a second drug. Using two drugs makes resistance slower to develop. In 2021 the World Health Organization recommended the first malaria *vaccine*, called RTS,S, for young children in areas with high malaria. A second vaccine, R21, followed in 2023. Neither is perfect, but together with nets they save lives.

words.d: a malaria drug first isolated from the sweet wormwood plant
treating a disease with two or more drugs at once so germs are less likely to become resistant
a product that trains the immune system to recognize a germ before a real infection

look.title: A Recipe From the Fourth Century
look.text: For intermittent fevers, take a handful of qinghao, soak it in about two liters of water, wring out the juice and drink all of it.
look.cite: Ge Hong, Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies, about 340 CE, as described by Tu Youyou in her 2015 Nobel lecture (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What detail in this old recipe helped Tu Youyou's team fix their method? What did they still have to do to prove the drug worked?

check.q: Why was Tu Youyou searching for a new malaria drug?
choices: There had never been any malaria drug
The parasite had become resistant to older drugs like chloroquine
check.why: The reading says older drugs such as chloroquine were failing because of resistance.

check.q: What clue from Ge Hong's text helped Tu's team?
choices: Boil the plant for a long time
Burn the plant and breathe the smoke
Soak the plant in water instead of boiling it
check.why: Ge Hong's recipe used soaking, not boiling, which led the team to a low-heat method.

check.q: Why do doctors combine artemisinin with a second drug?
choices: To slow the development of resistance
To make the pill taste better
To turn the drug into a vaccine
check.why: Combination therapy makes it harder for the parasite to become resistant.

lessons.title: Tuberculosis: An Old Disease
lessons.mainIdea: Tuberculosis is a bacterial lung infection that spreads through the air and can be cured with months of antibiotics.
reading: In 1882 the German doctor Robert Koch announced that he had found the germ behind *tuberculosis*, or TB. It is a bacterium now called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. At that time TB was one of the leading causes of death in Europe and the United States. People called it consumption because it seemed to waste the body away.

TB usually attacks the lungs. When a person with active TB in the lungs coughs, tiny droplets carry the bacteria into the air. Many people who breathe them in never become sick; the germ stays quiet in the body. This is called *latent TB*. Weak nutrition, crowded housing and HIV make it more likely that quiet TB turns into active disease.

Since the 1940s TB has been curable with *antibiotics*. The usual treatment takes about six months and uses several drugs at once. Stopping too early can let resistant bacteria survive. The World Health Organization reported that about 10.6 million people fell ill with TB in 2022. Most lived in low- and middle-income countries.

words.d: an infection caused by a bacterium that most often attacks the lungs
a TB infection in which the germ is in the body but is not causing illness
medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing

look.title: TB Around the World, 2022
rows: People who fell ill with TB
look.cite: World Health Organization, Global Tuberculosis Report 2023
look.prompt: About what fraction of the people who fell ill with TB in 2022 died of it? What does that tell you about how many were treated in time?

check.q: Who identified the bacterium that causes TB in 1882?
check.why: Robert Koch announced the discovery of the TB bacterium in 1882.

check.q: What is latent TB?
choices: TB that has spread to the brain
An infection where the germ is present but not causing illness
TB that has been fully cured
check.why: Latent TB means the germ stays quiet in the body without making the person sick.

check.q: Why is it important to finish the full course of TB drugs?
choices: Stopping early can let resistant bacteria survive
The last pills contain the vaccine
The drugs taste better over time
check.why: The reading warns that stopping too early can let resistant bacteria survive.

lessons.title: HIV and the Treatment Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: HIV has no cure yet, but daily antiretroviral therapy lets people live long, healthy lives and stops the virus from spreading through sex.
reading: In the early 1980s doctors in the United States noticed young adults falling ill with rare infections. Their immune systems had been badly weakened. Scientists identified the cause in 1983: a virus later named *HIV*, human immunodeficiency virus. Without treatment, HIV slowly destroys immune cells and can lead to AIDS, the most serious stage of the infection.

In 1996 researchers showed that combining three drugs could hold the virus down for years. This is *antiretroviral therapy*, or ART. A person taking ART every day can live a nearly normal lifespan. When the virus in the blood falls too low to measure, it is not passed on through sex. Health agencies sum this up as undetectable equals untransmittable.

At first ART cost thousands of dollars a year, far out of reach in poor countries. Cheaper generic drugs, and programs such as the Global Fund and the United States program PEPFAR, started in 2003, changed that. UNAIDS reported that by 2022 about 29.8 million of the roughly 39 million people with HIV were on treatment.

words.d: human immunodeficiency virus, which attacks immune cells
a daily combination of medicines that keeps HIV from multiplying
a lower-cost copy of a medicine that has the same active ingredient

look.title: HIV Worldwide, 2022
look.prompt: About how many people living with HIV were not yet on treatment in 2022? Why does reaching them matter for stopping new infections?

check.q: What does antiretroviral therapy do?
choices: It cures HIV in one week
It is a vaccine given at birth
It keeps HIV from multiplying when taken every day
check.why: ART is a daily drug combination that holds the virus down; it is not a cure.

check.q: What does undetectable equals untransmittable mean?
choices: People with very low virus levels on treatment do not pass HIV through sex
HIV cannot be found by any test
HIV is only spread by mosquitoes
Treatment makes a person immune to all viruses
check.why: When ART lowers the virus below measurable levels, it is not passed on through sex.

check.q: What helped bring ART to poorer countries?
choices: Cheaper generic drugs and programs like PEPFAR and the Global Fund
check.why: The reading names generic drugs, PEPFAR and the Global Fund as key changes.

lessons.title: Cholera and Clean Water
lessons.mainIdea: Cholera spreads through water tainted by human waste, so clean water and sanitation prevent it, and oral rehydration saves lives.
reading: In 1854 cholera struck the Soho district of London. The doctor *John Snow* marked each death on a map. The deaths clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump handle. He argued that cholera spread through dirty water, not bad air. Most experts at the time did not agree with him yet.

We now know cholera is caused by a bacterium carried in water or food tainted with human waste. It causes severe watery diarrhea, and a person can lose dangerous amounts of fluid within hours. The best protection is *sanitation*: safe toilets, sewers and treated drinking water. Chicago took a famous step in 1900, when engineers reversed the Chicago River so sewage flowed away from Lake Michigan, the city's water supply.

Treatment can be simple. *Oral rehydration solution* is clean water mixed with the right amounts of salt and sugar. The sugar helps the gut absorb the salt and water. Many doctors call it one of the most important medical advances of the twentieth century. Cholera outbreaks still happen where war, floods or poverty damage water systems.

words.d: a London doctor who traced an 1854 cholera outbreak to a water pump
safe ways of removing human waste, such as toilets and sewers
a drink of clean water with measured salt and sugar that replaces lost fluids

look.title: Snow's Argument
look.text: Snow wrote that nearly all the deaths had taken place a short distance from the Broad Street pump. Only a few deaths happened in houses nearer to a different pump. He concluded that the water from that pump was carrying the disease.
look.cite: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd edition, 1855 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What kind of evidence did Snow use? Why might a map convince people more than an argument alone?

check.q: How did John Snow find the source of the 1854 outbreak?
choices: He mapped the deaths and saw them cluster around one pump
He looked at the germ under a microscope
check.why: Snow marked deaths on a map and saw they clustered around the Broad Street pump.

check.q: Why did Chicago reverse its river in 1900?
choices: To send sewage away from its drinking water in Lake Michigan
To let ships reach the ocean faster
check.why: The reversal sent sewage away from Lake Michigan, the city's water supply.

check.q: Why does oral rehydration solution include sugar?
choices: To make the drink a vaccine
To help the gut absorb salt and water
To give the patient energy to exercise
check.why: The reading says sugar helps the gut absorb the salt and water.

lessons.title: Measles and the Power of Vaccines
lessons.mainIdea: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases, and two doses of vaccine protect about 97 out of 100 people.
reading: *Measles* is caused by a virus that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The virus can hang in the air of a room for up to two hours. It causes a high fever and a rash, and it can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and death, especially in young children and people who are poorly nourished.

A measles vaccine was licensed in the United States in 1963. Today most children receive it as part of the MMR shot, which also protects against mumps and rubella. The CDC reports that two doses are about 97 percent effective at preventing measles. In 2000 the United States declared measles eliminated, meaning it no longer spread year-round inside the country.

When enough people in a community are protected, the virus cannot find new people to infect. This is called *herd immunity*. It also shields babies who are too young for the shot. Because measles spreads so easily, about 95 percent of people need to be immune. When vaccination rates drop, outbreaks return, as happened in several U.S. states in 2019.

words.d: a very contagious viral disease that causes fever and a rash
protection for a whole community when enough people are immune that a germ cannot spread
no longer spreading year-round in one country or region, though cases can arrive from elsewhere

look.title: A Classroom of Thirty
look.text: In a class of thirty students, twenty-nine have had two doses of MMR vaccine. One student has a medical condition and cannot get the vaccine. A visitor with measles walks through the school.
look.prompt: How does the vaccination of the twenty-nine help protect the one? What would change if only fifteen were vaccinated?

check.q: About how effective are two doses of measles vaccine, according to the CDC?
check.why: The CDC reports that two doses are about 97 percent effective.

check.q: What is herd immunity?
choices: Protection for a community when enough people are immune that a germ cannot spread
Immunity that comes only from farm animals
Protection that lasts only one day
check.why: Herd immunity means enough people are immune that the germ cannot keep spreading.

check.q: What did it mean when the U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000?
choices: No one anywhere could catch measles
Measles no longer spread year-round inside the country
The vaccine was no longer needed
check.why: Eliminated means no year-round spread within one country; cases can still arrive from abroad.

lessons.title: Neglected Tropical Diseases
lessons.mainIdea: Neglected tropical diseases affect over a billion of the world's poorest people, and some, like Guinea worm, are close to being wiped out.
reading: Some diseases get little attention in wealthy countries because they rarely appear there. The World Health Organization groups about twenty of them as *neglected tropical diseases*. They include river blindness, sleeping sickness, schistosomiasis and intestinal worms. Together they affect more than one billion people, mostly in poor, rural areas with little clean water.

These diseases often do not kill quickly. Instead they cause blindness, pain, tiredness and disability that can keep children out of school and adults out of work. Some can be treated with cheap pills given to whole communities once or twice a year. This approach is called *mass drug administration*. Drug companies have donated billions of doses.

*Guinea worm disease* shows what steady work can do. People catch it by drinking water that holds tiny water fleas carrying the worm's larvae. There is no vaccine or medicine for it. Instead, villages filter their water and keep people with emerging worms out of ponds. The Carter Center reported about 3.5 million cases in 1986 and only 14 human cases in 2023.

words.d: a group of diseases that mainly affect poor communities in warm regions and get little funding
giving medicine to everyone in an at-risk community, not only to people who feel sick
a parasitic disease caught from drinking unfiltered water that holds worm larvae

look.title: Guinea Worm Cases
look.cite: The Carter Center and World Health Organization, Guinea Worm Eradication Program reports
look.prompt: Guinea worm was pushed down without any vaccine or drug. What does that tell you about the power of clean water and community work?

check.q: Why are some diseases called neglected?
choices: They affect mostly poor communities and get little attention or funding
They cannot be treated in any way
check.why: They mainly affect poor, rural people and get little attention in wealthy countries.

check.q: What is mass drug administration?
choices: Giving medicine only to people in hospitals
Giving medicine to everyone in an at-risk community
check.why: It means treating whole communities, not only people who feel sick.

check.q: How has Guinea worm been reduced without a vaccine or drug?
choices: By filtering water and keeping people with worms out of ponds
check.why: Villages filter water and keep people with emerging worms from contaminating ponds.

lessons.title: Polio, Nearly Gone
lessons.mainIdea: Vaccines have cut wild polio cases by more than 99 percent since 1988, leaving only a few places where it still spreads.
reading: In the early 1950s summer brought fear to American families. *Polio*, a virus that can paralyze, closed swimming pools and filled hospital wards. In 1955 a vaccine made by Jonas Salk was declared safe and effective. A few years later Albert Sabin developed an oral vaccine given as drops, which was easier to use in large campaigns.

In 1988 the World Health Assembly launched the Global Polio Eradication Initiative. At that time polio paralyzed about 350,000 children a year in more than 125 countries. Health workers went village by village, even into war zones, giving drops to every child under five. Cases fell by more than 99 percent.

*Eradication* means wiping a disease out everywhere, for good. Only one human disease, smallpox, has been eradicated, confirmed in 1980. Wild polio still spreads in parts of Pakistan and Afghanistan. Conflict, distrust and hard-to-reach communities are the main obstacles. Rich countries stay at risk until polio is gone everywhere, because a traveler can carry it across borders.

words.d: a viral disease that can cause paralysis, mainly in young children
wiping out a disease everywhere in the world permanently
a vaccine given by mouth, such as drops, instead of by a shot

look.title: Wild Polio Cases
look.cite: Global Polio Eradication Initiative, case counts
look.prompt: Cases dropped fastest in the early years. Why might the last few cases be the hardest to stop?

check.q: Who developed the oral polio vaccine given as drops?
check.why: Albert Sabin developed the oral vaccine; Jonas Salk made the earlier injected vaccine.

check.q: What is the difference between elimination and eradication?
choices: Eradication means a disease is gone everywhere for good
Elimination means gone from the whole world
check.why: Eradication is worldwide and permanent; elimination applies to one country or region.

check.q: Which human disease has already been eradicated?
check.why: Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated so far, confirmed in 1980.

sections.title: Who Gets Sick, and Who Helps

lessons.title: Global Health Organizations
lessons.mainIdea: The WHO sets health guidance for the world, while groups like Gavi and the Global Fund pay for vaccines and treatment in poorer countries.
reading: After World War II, nations created the *World Health Organization*, or WHO, in 1948. It is a United Nations agency based in Geneva, Switzerland. The WHO does not run hospitals in most countries. Instead it gathers data, writes guidelines, tracks outbreaks and helps governments plan. It led the campaign that eradicated smallpox.

Newer groups mostly raise and spend money. *Gavi*, the Vaccine Alliance, began in 2000. It helps low-income countries buy vaccines at lower prices, and it reports helping vaccinate more than a billion children. The *Global Fund*, created in 2002, pays for programs against AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria. Governments, foundations and companies give to both.

These groups do not always agree, and they face hard choices. Money is limited. Donors may prefer one disease over another. Some critics say global programs should do more to build local health systems instead of fighting one disease at a time. Supporters answer that focused programs show clear results. Both sides want the same goal: fewer people dying of preventable causes.

words.d: the United Nations agency, founded in 1948, that guides global public health
an alliance, begun in 2000, that helps low-income countries buy and deliver vaccines
a partnership, created in 2002, that pays for programs against AIDS, TB and malaria

look.title: How the WHO Defines Health
look.text: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
look.cite: Constitution of the World Health Organization, signed 1946, in force 1948
look.prompt: This definition includes social well-being. Why might a global health group care about housing, clean water or schooling, not just medicine?

check.q: What is the main job of the World Health Organization?
choices: Running every hospital in the world
Gathering data, writing guidelines and tracking outbreaks
check.why: The WHO gathers data, writes guidelines, tracks outbreaks and helps governments plan.

check.q: Which group mainly helps low-income countries buy vaccines?
check.why: Gavi, begun in 2000, focuses on helping countries buy and deliver vaccines.

check.q: What is one criticism of disease-by-disease programs?
choices: They should do more to build whole local health systems
They spend too little on malaria
They only work in wealthy countries
check.why: Some critics say programs should strengthen local health systems, not fight one disease at a time.

lessons.title: Poverty, Place and Disease
lessons.mainIdea: Where people live and how much money they have strongly shape which diseases they catch and whether they get treated.
reading: Malaria once spread in parts of the United States, including along rivers in Illinois. It faded in the twentieth century as swamps were drained, homes got screens and people could afford doctors. The mosquitoes that can carry it still live in the country. What changed was mostly housing, money and health care, not the insects.

*Geography* matters too. Anopheles mosquitoes need warm weather and standing water, so malaria is heaviest in tropical regions. Cholera follows broken water systems. TB spreads in crowded rooms. But geography alone does not decide who gets sick. Poverty often decides whether a family has screens, clean water, enough food and a clinic nearby.

Public health experts call these conditions the *social determinants of health*. They include income, schooling, housing, clean water and safe work. A child born in a wealthy country today can expect to live many years longer than a child born in the poorest countries. Closing that gap takes medicine, but also roads, schools, clean water and fair economies.

the conditions where people live, learn and work, such as income and housing, that shape health
work that protects the health of whole communities, not only one patient

chapters.title: Chronic Disease and Lifestyle
chapters.bigQuestion: How much of our long-term health is shaped by daily habits, and how much by the places and cultures we live in?

story.title: The Island of Long Lives
story.kicker: On Okinawa, researchers met people past one hundred and asked what their lives had been like.
paragraphs: In 1975 a Japanese doctor named Makoto Suzuki began a study on Okinawa, a chain of islands in the far south of Japan. He had noticed that an unusual number of older people there were living past one hundred. Many of them were still gardening, walking to see friends and caring for grandchildren.

Suzuki and later researchers visited homes and checked birth records. They measured blood pressure and asked people what they ate. Older Okinawans described meals built around sweet potatoes, green vegetables, tofu and seaweed. Meat, often pork, was saved mostly for festivals. Many had grown up with a saying, hara hachi bu: eat until you are about eight parts out of ten full.

The researchers also noticed things that were not on a plate. Older people stayed active in their gardens and fields. Many belonged to a moai, a small group of friends who met for years and helped one another. Rates of heart disease and some cancers among older Okinawans were lower than in many other wealthy places at that time.

Then the islands changed. After World War II, American bases and fast-food restaurants brought new foods. Younger Okinawans began eating more meat, fat and processed food, and moving less. By the early 2000s, Okinawa's long-life advantage among younger adults had largely faded. The study raised a big question: what really keeps people healthy over a whole lifetime?
story.think: The older Okinawans had healthy habits, but so much changed for their grandchildren. What does that suggest about whether health is only a matter of personal choice?

lessons.title: Heart Disease and Stroke
lessons.mainIdea: Heart disease and stroke, both caused mostly by damaged blood vessels, are the two leading causes of death in the world.
reading: A *chronic disease* lasts a long time and usually develops slowly. Heart disease, stroke, cancer, diabetes and long-term lung disease are the main examples. The World Health Organization reports that these noncommunicable diseases cause about 41 million deaths a year. That is roughly three out of every four deaths worldwide.

The most common kind of heart disease starts when fatty deposits called *plaque* build up inside the arteries that feed the heart. The arteries narrow and stiffen. If a clot forms on the plaque and blocks blood flow, part of the heart muscle is starved of oxygen. That is a heart attack. It often causes chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath and sweating.

A *stroke* is the same kind of problem in the brain. Most strokes happen when a clot blocks an artery to the brain; some happen when a blood vessel bursts. Brain cells begin to die within minutes. Quick care matters, so health groups teach the signs: a drooping face, a weak arm, and slurred speech mean call emergency services right away.

words.d: an illness that lasts a long time and usually develops slowly
a fatty buildup inside an artery that narrows it
damage to the brain when its blood supply is blocked or a vessel bursts

look.title: Top Causes of Death Worldwide, 2019
look.cite: World Health Organization, Global Health Estimates, The Top 10 Causes of Death, 2020
look.prompt: Together, what share of deaths do heart disease and stroke cause? Why might they be grouped together?

check.q: What is a chronic disease?
choices: An illness that spreads through mosquitoes
An illness that lasts a long time and develops slowly
An illness that lasts only one day
An infection cured in a week
check.why: The reading defines a chronic disease as one that lasts a long time and develops slowly.

check.q: What usually causes a heart attack?
choices: A clot blocking an artery narrowed by plaque
Too much water in the blood
check.why: A clot on plaque blocks blood flow and starves part of the heart muscle of oxygen.

check.q: Why do health groups teach the signs of a stroke?
choices: Brain cells begin to die within minutes, so quick care matters

check.why: Brain cells begin to die within minutes, so calling for help fast matters.

lessons.title: Cancer
lessons.mainIdea: Cancer is a group of diseases in which cells grow out of control, and some cancers can be prevented or caught early.
reading: Your body replaces old cells with new ones all the time. Each cell follows instructions in its DNA about when to divide and when to stop. Sometimes changes in the DNA, called *mutations*, break those instructions. A cell may keep dividing when it should not. Over time it can form a lump called a *tumor*.

Cancer is not one disease but more than a hundred. Lung, breast, colon and prostate cancer are among the most common worldwide. Some tumors are benign, meaning they do not spread. Cancer is the name for tumors that invade nearby tissue and can travel through the body, which doctors call *metastasis*.

Some mutations come from chance as cells copy their DNA. Others come from outside causes. Tobacco smoke is the single largest preventable cause of cancer. Too much sun raises the risk of skin cancer. Some infections play a role too; the HPV vaccine protects against most cervical cancers. Treatments include surgery, radiation and medicines, and many cancers found early can be treated successfully.

words.d: changes in a cell's DNA instructions
a lump formed when cells divide more than they should
the spread of cancer cells from where they started to other parts of the body

look.title: Cancer Worldwide, 2020
look.cite: International Agency for Research on Cancer, GLOBOCAN 2020
look.prompt: About how many new cancer cases were there for every cancer death? What might explain why many people survive?

check.q: What is metastasis?
choices: A benign tumor that stays in place
The spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body
check.why: Metastasis means cancer cells travel from where they began to other parts of the body.

check.q: What does the reading name as the largest preventable cause of cancer?
check.why: The reading says tobacco smoke is the single largest preventable cause of cancer.

check.q: Which vaccine protects against most cervical cancers?
check.why: The HPV vaccine guards against the virus behind most cervical cancers.

lessons.title: Diabetes
lessons.mainIdea: Diabetes means the body cannot use sugar in the blood well; type 2, the most common kind, is strongly linked to lifestyle and can often be delayed or prevented.
reading: When you eat, your body breaks much of your food into a sugar called glucose. It travels in the blood to feed your cells. A hormone called *insulin*, made by the pancreas, acts like a key that lets glucose into the cells. *Diabetes* means this system is not working, so sugar builds up in the blood.

In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin. It often begins in childhood, and people need insulin every day. Insulin was first used to treat patients in 1922 in Toronto, after work by Frederick Banting, Charles Best and others. Before then, type 1 diabetes was nearly always fatal.

*Type 2 diabetes* makes up about nine out of ten cases. The body still makes insulin but does not respond to it well. Family history plays a part, but so do weight, diet and activity. Large studies found that regular activity and modest weight loss can delay or prevent it in many at-risk adults. Over time, high blood sugar can harm the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart.

words.d: a hormone from the pancreas that lets glucose move from the blood into cells
a long-term condition in which blood sugar stays too high
the most common form of diabetes, in which the body does not respond well to insulin

look.title: Two Kinds, Two Stories
look.text: Maya is eleven. She was thirsty all the time and lost weight without trying. Tests showed her body had stopped making insulin. Her uncle is fifty-five. At a checkup, his blood sugar was high, though he felt fine. His body still makes insulin but does not respond well to it.
look.prompt: Which type of diabetes does each person likely have? Which one might daily habits help most, and why?

check.q: What does insulin do?
choices: It breaks down fat in the stomach
It lets glucose move from the blood into cells
It carries oxygen in the blood
check.why: Insulin acts like a key that lets glucose into cells.

check.q: How does type 1 diabetes differ from type 2?
choices: Type 1 is caused by eating sugar; type 2 is caused by a virus
In type 1 the immune system destroys insulin-making cells; in type 2 the body responds poorly to insulin
check.why: Type 1 comes from immune damage to insulin-making cells; type 2 from poor response to insulin.

check.q: What did large studies find could delay or prevent type 2 diabetes in many at-risk adults?
choices: Regular activity and modest weight loss
check.why: The reading says regular activity and modest weight loss can delay or prevent it for many.

lessons.title: Tobacco and Smoking
lessons.mainIdea: Tobacco is the leading preventable cause of death worldwide, and quitting at any age lowers the risk.
reading: In the 1950s, researchers in Britain and the United States compared people with lung cancer to people without it. Smokers turned up far more often among the patients. In 1964 the U.S. Surgeon General issued a report concluding that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer in men. It was a turning point in public health.

A *risk factor* is anything that raises the chance of getting a disease. Tobacco is a risk factor for heart disease, stroke, many cancers and lung disease. The World Health Organization estimates that tobacco causes more than 8 million deaths a year, including about 1.3 million people who do not smoke but breathe *secondhand smoke*. Nicotine, the chemical in tobacco, is highly *addictive*.

Smoking rates in the United States have fallen by more than half since the 1960s. Taxes, smoke-free laws, warning labels and support to quit all helped. Vaping devices also deliver nicotine, and health agencies advise young people not to use them. The good news is clear: the body starts to recover soon after a person quits, and help is available from doctors and quit lines.

words.d: anything that raises the chance of getting a disease
smoke breathed in by people near someone who is smoking
causing a strong need to keep using something even when a person wants to stop

look.title: The 1964 Report
look.text: Cigarette smoking is causally related to lung cancer in men. The size of the effect of smoking far outweighs all other factors.
look.cite: U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory Committee, Smoking and Health, 1964 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: The report was based on many studies comparing groups of people. Why was it important to find the same result again and again?

check.q: What is a risk factor?
choices: A disease that is always fatal
Anything that raises the chance of getting a disease
check.why: A risk factor is anything that raises the chance of disease.

check.q: What did the 1964 Surgeon General's report conclude?
choices: Smoking causes lung cancer in men
check.why: The report concluded that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer in men.

check.q: What does the reading say about quitting smoking?
choices: It only helps people under twenty
The body starts to recover soon after quitting
It makes no difference after age forty
It is impossible to get help
check.why: The reading says the body starts to recover soon after a person quits.

lessons.title: Blood Pressure: The Quiet Risk
lessons.mainIdea: High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so regular checks matter, and it can be lowered with habits and medicine.
reading: Each time your heart beats, it pushes blood against the walls of your arteries. *Blood pressure* is the force of that push. A nurse measures it with a cuff and writes two numbers, such as 118 over 76. The top number is the pressure during a heartbeat; the bottom is the pressure between beats.

When pressure stays too high for a long time, it strains the heart and damages arteries. This is called *hypertension*. It is a leading risk factor for heart attack and stroke. Most people with hypertension feel perfectly fine, which is why doctors call it a silent condition. The only way to know is to measure it.

The World Health Organization reported in 2023 that about 1.3 billion adults aged 30 to 79 have hypertension, and nearly half do not know it. Less salt, more activity, less alcohol and not smoking all help. Many people also need daily medicine. A research program in the 1940s, the Framingham Heart Study in Massachusetts, helped show how strongly blood pressure predicts heart disease.

words.d: the force of blood pushing against the walls of the arteries
blood pressure that stays too high over time
a long-running study, begun in 1948 in Massachusetts, that identified major risk factors for heart disease

look.title: Reading the Cuff
look.text: At a health fair, three adults get their blood pressure checked. Ana reads 116 over 74. Ben reads 148 over 94, but he says he feels great. Carla reads 128 over 78. The nurse gives Ben a card suggesting he see a doctor soon.
look.prompt: Why does the nurse send Ben to a doctor even though he feels fine? What does this tell you about the value of checkups?

check.q: Why is hypertension called a silent condition?
choices: It makes the heart stop beating
Most people with it feel fine and have no symptoms
check.why: Most people with hypertension feel fine, so it must be measured to be found.

check.q: In a reading of 118 over 76, what does 118 stand for?
check.why: The top number is the pressure while the heart is beating.

check.q: Which study helped show how strongly blood pressure predicts heart disease?
check.why: The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948, identified blood pressure as a major risk factor.

lessons.title: Food and Movement
lessons.mainIdea: Eating mostly whole foods and staying active lower the risk of most chronic diseases.
reading: Nutrition scientists agree on a few broad patterns. Diets rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans and nuts are linked to lower rates of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers. Diets high in sugary drinks, *processed meat* and salty packaged foods are linked to higher rates. Scientists still debate many details, such as exactly how much fat or which kinds are best.

Much of the salt people eat comes not from the salt shaker but from bread, canned soups, chips and restaurant food. Too much salt raises blood pressure in many people. *Ultra-processed foods*, made mostly from refined ingredients and additives, are easy to overeat and are a growing share of diets in many countries.

Moving your body matters as much as food. *Physical activity* strengthens the heart, helps control blood sugar and blood pressure, and improves mood and sleep. The World Health Organization recommends that children and teens get an average of at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity a day. Walking, dancing, biking, sports and active chores all count.

words.d: meat preserved by salting, curing or smoking, such as bacon, hot dogs and ham
factory-made foods built mostly from refined ingredients and additives
any body movement that uses energy, from walking to sports

look.title: How Much Activity?
look.cite: World Health Organization, Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020
look.prompt: Turn the teen goal into minutes per week. How does it compare with the adult goals?

check.q: Where does much of the salt people eat come from?
choices: Bread, canned soups, chips and restaurant food
check.why: The reading says most salt comes from packaged and restaurant foods, not the shaker.

check.q: How much activity does the WHO recommend for children and teens?
choices: At least 60 minutes a day on average
check.why: The WHO recommends an average of at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity a day.

check.q: What does the reading say scientists still debate?
choices: Details such as how much fat or which kinds are best
check.why: Broad patterns are agreed on, but details like fat amounts and types are still debated.

lessons.title: What Okinawa Taught
lessons.mainIdea: Traditional Okinawan life combined a plant-rich, modest-calorie diet with activity and close friendships, and the benefits faded when those habits changed.
reading: The Okinawa Centenarian Study, begun by Makoto Suzuki in 1975, followed hundreds of people aged one hundred or older. Researchers found that older Okinawans had eaten a traditional diet based on sweet potatoes, vegetables, soy foods and some fish. Calories were modest. Many practiced *hara hachi bu*, stopping before they felt completely full.

The diet was only part of the picture. Older Okinawans kept working in gardens and fields into old age. Many belonged to a *moai*, a group of friends who met regularly for life and supported one another. Researchers think purpose, friendship and daily movement may matter along with food, though separating each piece is hard.

Scientists are careful about what one place can prove. People who live long may share genes as well as habits. Some researchers have questioned how accurate very old birth records were in several long-lived regions. The strongest clue is what happened next: as younger Okinawans ate more fast food and moved less, their health advantage shrank. That change points to *lifestyle*, not genes alone.

words.d: an Okinawan saying that means eat until you are about eight parts out of ten full
in Okinawa, a small group of friends who meet and support one another for life
the everyday habits of a person or group, such as eating, moving and resting

look.title: Grandmother and Grandson
look.text: An Okinawan grandmother, born in 1920, ate sweet potatoes and vegetables from her garden and walked everywhere. Her grandson, born in 1985, grew up near a burger restaurant and drives to work. Both share much of the same family DNA.
look.prompt: If the grandson's health is worse at fifty than his grandmother's was, what does that suggest about genes and lifestyle? What else might you need to know before deciding?

check.q: What is hara hachi bu?
choices: An Okinawan saying about eating until about 80 percent full
check.why: Hara hachi bu means stopping when you are about eight parts out of ten full.

check.q: Why do researchers think lifestyle, not only genes, mattered in Okinawa?
choices: Okinawans have no genes in common
The health advantage shrank when younger people's habits changed
check.why: The advantage faded as habits changed within the same families, pointing to lifestyle.

check.q: What is one reason scientists are careful about long-life claims?
choices: Okinawa is too small to visit
No one has ever lived to one hundred
Some have questioned how accurate very old birth records are
check.why: The reading notes questions about the accuracy of very old birth records.

lessons.title: The Mediterranean Diet
lessons.mainIdea: The traditional Mediterranean way of eating has been linked in studies to less heart disease, though researchers debate how strong the evidence is.
reading: In the 1950s the American scientist Ancel Keys noticed that heart attacks seemed rare in parts of southern Italy and on the Greek island of Crete. In 1958 he began the *Seven Countries Study*, comparing men in the United States, Finland, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Yugoslavia and Japan. Men in Crete and Japan had some of the lowest rates of heart disease.

The *Mediterranean diet*, as later studies described it, features vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts, fish and olive oil, with little red meat or sweets. Meals are often shared slowly with family. In 2010 UNESCO listed the Mediterranean diet as part of the cultural heritage of humanity, honoring its traditions of farming, cooking and eating together.

A large Spanish trial called PREDIMED, published in 2013, found fewer heart attacks and strokes among people told to eat this way with extra olive oil or nuts. In 2018 the authors withdrew and reissued the paper after finding problems in how some people were assigned to groups. The new analysis found similar results, but with more caution. Many experts still see this pattern as healthy, while debating how much each part matters. This is how *evidence* grows and gets tested.

words.d: a study begun in 1958 by Ancel Keys that compared diet and heart disease in seven countries
a traditional way of eating built on vegetables, beans, whole grains, fish and olive oil
facts and results from observation and testing that support or weaken an idea

look.title: Comparing Two Traditions
look.text: Traditional Okinawan meal: sweet potato, stir-fried greens, tofu, miso soup, a little fish. Traditional Cretan meal: bean stew with tomatoes, wild greens with olive oil, bread, a little cheese, fruit. Both are eaten with family or neighbors.
look.prompt: Name two things these very different meals have in common. Why might researchers find it useful that different cultures reached similar patterns?

check.q: Who began the Seven Countries Study in 1958?
check.why: Ancel Keys began the Seven Countries Study in 1958.

check.q: What happened to the PREDIMED paper in 2018?
choices: It was withdrawn and reissued after problems with group assignment were found
check.why: The authors withdrew and reissued it; the new analysis found similar but more cautious results.

check.q: Which foods are central to the Mediterranean diet?
choices: Vegetables, beans, whole grains, fish and olive oil
check.why: The reading lists vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts, fish and olive oil.

lessons.title: Food Environments
lessons.mainIdea: The food that is nearby, cheap and advertised shapes what people eat, so healthy choices are easier in some places than others.
reading: Imagine two students walking home from school. One passes a grocery store with fresh fruit and a park with a basketball court. The other passes three fast-food restaurants and a gas station, with no store selling fresh produce for a mile. Both students want to eat well, but their choices are not the same.

Researchers call these surroundings a *food environment*: the stores, restaurants, prices and advertising around a person. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has studied areas where many people live far from a supermarket and have low incomes. These areas are sometimes called *food deserts*. People living there often rely on small stores with more packaged food.

Food environments can be changed. Some cities offer incentives for grocery stores to open in underserved neighborhoods. Schools can serve healthier lunches and put water fountains in easy reach. Farmers markets can accept food assistance benefits. Researchers still debate which changes help most, since a new store does not always change what people buy. But the idea is clear: *access* shapes habits.

words.d: the stores, restaurants, prices and advertising that surround a person
areas where many people have low incomes and live far from a supermarket
being able to reach and afford something, such as healthy food or a doctor

look.title: Map Your Route
look.text: Think about the route you take home from school. Count the places where you could buy food. How many sell fresh fruit or vegetables? How many sell mostly chips, candy or fried food? Where is the nearest place to get free drinking water?
look.prompt: Describe your own food environment. What is one change in your neighborhood or school that would make a healthy choice easier?

check.q: What is a food environment?
choices: The stores, restaurants, prices and advertising around a person
The part of the stomach that digests food
check.why: A food environment includes the stores, restaurants, prices and ads around a person.

check.q: What makes an area a food desert, as the USDA describes it?
choices: Many people have low incomes and live far from a supermarket
It has too many grocery stores
check.why: The USDA looks at low income and long distance to a supermarket.

check.q: Why do researchers still debate how to improve food environments?
choices: A new store does not always change what people buy
check.why: The reading notes that opening a store does not always change buying habits.

lessons.title: Screening: Finding Disease Early
lessons.mainIdea: Screening tests look for disease before symptoms appear, which can save lives, but every test has trade-offs.
reading: In the 1940s the Greek-American doctor George Papanicolaou showed that looking at cells from the cervix under a microscope could reveal early signs of cancer. His test, the *Pap test*, became routine. Deaths from cervical cancer in the United States fell sharply in the following decades, in large part because early changes were found and treated.

*Screening* means testing people who feel well to find a disease early. Blood pressure checks, blood sugar tests, mammograms for breast cancer and colonoscopies for colon cancer are examples. Finding a cancer while it is small often makes treatment simpler and more successful.

Screening is not free of problems. A *false positive* is a result that suggests disease when none is there, which can bring worry and more tests. Some screening finds slow cancers that would never have caused harm. That is why expert groups weigh benefits and harms and sometimes disagree about the best age to start a test. Patients decide with their doctors.

words.d: testing people without symptoms to find a disease early
a test that checks cells from the cervix for early signs of cancer
a test result that shows a disease when the person does not have it

look.title: Weighing a Test
look.text: A new screening test finds a certain cancer early in 9 of 10 people who have it. But in a large group of healthy people, it also flags a few out of every hundred as possible cancer, and they need more tests to learn they are fine.
look.prompt: List one benefit and one harm of this test. What would you want to ask a doctor before deciding to take it?

check.q: What is screening?
choices: Treating a disease after symptoms appear
Testing people who feel well to find disease early
check.why: Screening means testing people without symptoms to catch disease early.

check.q: What did George Papanicolaou's test look for?
choices: Early signs of cervical cancer in cells
check.why: The Pap test checks cervical cells for early signs of cancer.

check.q: What is a false positive?
choices: A test that is never used
A result showing disease when none is present
check.why: A false positive suggests disease when the person does not have it.

lessons.title: Prevention or Treatment?
lessons.mainIdea: Preventing disease across a whole population can save more lives than treating each sick person, though both are needed.
reading: In 1972 the region of North Karelia in Finland had one of the highest rates of heart disease deaths in the world. Local leaders and health workers launched a community project. They worked with farmers, food companies, schools and shops to cut salt and saturated fat, promote vegetables and help people quit smoking. Over the following decades, heart disease deaths among working-age men there fell dramatically.

This is *prevention*: stopping disease before it starts. Treatment helps people who are already sick, with medicines, surgery or care. Both matter. A person having a heart attack needs a hospital now. But a community that lowers everyone's blood pressure a little may prevent many heart attacks from ever happening.

The British epidemiologist Geoffrey Rose called this the *prevention paradox*. A small change across a whole population can prevent many cases, yet each single person may notice little benefit. That can make prevention hard to value, because the people it helps never know they were spared. Societies debate how much to spend on each side and how far governments should go in shaping choices like food and tobacco.

words.d: actions that stop a disease before it starts
the idea that small changes across a population prevent many cases, though each person gains little they can see
a scientist who studies how diseases spread and what causes them in groups of people

look.title: Rose's Paradox
look.text: A preventive measure that brings large benefits to the whole community may offer little to each individual person who takes part.
look.cite: Geoffrey Rose, Strategy of Prevention: Lessons From Cardiovascular Disease, British Medical Journal, 1981 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Think of seat belts or lower salt in bread. How does Rose's idea explain why some people see little reason to change, even when the whole community gains?

check.q: What did the North Karelia Project in Finland focus on?
choices: Community changes to cut salt, fat and smoking
check.why: The project worked with farmers, food companies, schools and shops to change habits across the region.

check.q: What is the prevention paradox?
choices: Treatment is always cheaper than prevention
Only sick people benefit from prevention
Small changes across a population prevent many cases, though each person sees little benefit
check.why: Geoffrey Rose described how population-wide prevention helps many while each person notices little.

check.q: What does an epidemiologist study?
choices: How diseases spread and what causes them in groups of people
Only the bones of the body
check.why: An epidemiologist studies patterns and causes of disease in groups.

lessons.title: Culture, Food and Movement
lessons.mainIdea: Culture shapes how people eat and move, and healthy habits last longest when they fit a community's own traditions.
reading: In Japan, most elementary and junior high schools serve lunch planned with trained nutritionists. Students often serve the food to classmates and eat together in the classroom. The meals follow *washoku*, the traditional Japanese way of eating, which UNESCO recognized as cultural heritage in 2013. Eating becomes a shared lesson, not just a break.

*Culture* is the shared beliefs, habits and traditions of a group. It shapes which foods feel like home, when families eat, whether people walk or drive, and how celebrations are marked. Traditional medical systems carry cultural ideas about food too. Ayurveda, for example, teaches choosing foods to keep the body's doshas in balance, an idea from that tradition rather than a measured fact.

Health programs work better when they respect culture. A program that tells a family to give up its favorite dishes often fails. A program that helps cook those dishes with less salt, or that builds on a tradition of walking to market, has a better chance. Health workers who come from the community, like the health worker in Kenya, often know what will fit.

words.d: the shared beliefs, habits and traditions of a group of people
the traditional Japanese way of preparing and eating food, recognized by UNESCO in 2013
a custom or belief passed down from one generation to the next

look.title: Two Health Messages
look.text: Message A: Stop eating your family's traditional dishes; they are unhealthy. Message B: Here are three ways to cook your family's favorite dishes with more vegetables and less salt, shared by cooks from your neighborhood.
look.prompt: Which message is more likely to change habits over time? Use the idea of culture to explain your answer.

check.q: What is washoku?
choices: The traditional Japanese way of preparing and eating food
check.why: Washoku is the traditional Japanese way of eating, recognized by UNESCO in 2013.

check.q: How does the reading describe the Ayurvedic idea of doshas?
choices: As a proven measurement in blood tests
As an idea from that tradition rather than a measured fact
As a type of food desert
check.why: The reading presents doshas as Ayurveda's own idea, not a measured fact.

check.q: Why do health programs work better when they respect culture?
choices: They fit what people already value, so changes are more likely to last
Culture has no effect on eating
They avoid talking about food at all
They require people to move away
check.why: Building on familiar traditions makes new habits easier to keep.

review.q: What are the two leading causes of death worldwide?
review.why: WHO estimates rank ischemic heart disease first and stroke second.

review.q: Which is a risk factor for heart disease?
review.why: Smoking raises the chance of heart disease; the others lower risk.

review.q: How do the Okinawan and Mediterranean diets compare?
choices: Both are plant-rich traditional patterns linked to less heart disease
Both are built on red meat
review.why: Both are traditional, plant-rich patterns that studies have linked to lower heart disease.

review.q: Why is blood pressure checked even when people feel well?
choices: High blood pressure cannot be treated
review.why: Hypertension is usually silent, so measuring is the only way to find it.

review.q: What happened to Okinawa's health advantage as habits changed?
review.why: As younger Okinawans ate more fast food and moved less, the advantage faded.

review.q: Which example shows prevention rather than treatment?
choices: Lowering salt in foods across a region
Insulin for a person with type 1 diabetes
review.why: Cutting salt across a region stops disease before it starts, as in North Karelia.

review.q: What is a trade-off of screening tests?
choices: They can give false positives that lead to worry and more tests
They are only for sick people
review.why: Screening can catch disease early but also gives false positives.

choices: A dry region with no farms
An area where many low-income people live far from a supermarket
review.why: The USDA uses low income and distance to a supermarket to describe these areas.
